output.content:
**Arm fiscal 2026 (year ended March 31, 2026): data-center deployment takeaways.** [[1]]

- Arm reported that cumulative **Neoverse deployments surpassed 1 billion CPU cores** during FYE26, spanning general-purpose and custom cloud silicon, including NVIDIA Grace, AWS Graviton, Google Axion, and Microsoft Cobalt. [[2]]
- Arm expected its CPUs to reach **nearly 50% of deployments among leading hyperscalers** during the year; by the FYE26 full-year release, it characterized its CPU-compute share among top hyperscalers as **about 50%**. [[2]] [[1]]
- The company cited increasing use of Neoverse CPUs as **host/head nodes paired with AI accelerators** for training and inference, a strategic driver of data-center CPU content as AI clusters scale. [[2]]
- Financially, Arm reported that **data-center royalty revenue more than doubled year over year in FYE26**, contributing to record full-year royalty revenue of **$2.61 billion**. [[1]]

**AWS / Graviton specifically.** [[3]]

- AWS launched fifth-generation **Graviton5**, using **192 cores**, versus 96 cores in Graviton4—i.e., a doubling of core count—and Arm said the product delivered up to **25% higher performance** and **33% lower latency** than Graviton4. [[3]]
- Arm identified Graviton5 as built on the higher-performance **Neoverse CSS V3** platform, alongside AWS’s use of Arm-based Nitro DPUs and Trainium accelerators in an integrated cloud system design. [[4]]
- Arm also reported that AWS’s broader custom-silicon business—encompassing **Graviton, Trainium, and Nitro**—was running at **more than $20 billion annually** and growing triple digits year over year. [[1]]
- The deployment implication is that AWS is not merely offering Arm instances as a niche alternative: Graviton’s higher core density and integration with AWS’s accelerator/networking stack support Arm’s expanding share of hyperscale AI and general-purpose compute. [[3]] [[2]]
